'''Martin Jacob Jackley'''<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.legistorm.com/person/bio/469462/Martin_Jacob_Jackley.html |title=Marty Jackley - South Dakota Office of the Attorney General |website= LegiStorm}}</ref> (born October 13, 1970) is an American attorney and politician who is serving as the [[Attorney General of South Dakota]] since 2023, having previously served from 2009 to 2019. He assumed office as Attorney General again in 2023 after winning the 2022 election unopposed. He previously served as the 39th [[United States Attorney for the District of South Dakota|United States Attorney]] for the [[United States District Court for the District of South Dakota|District of South Dakota]].  He ran unsuccessfully for Governor of South Dakota in 2018, losing the Republican primary to [[Kristi Noem]].

In 2026, Jackley declined to run for re-election to a fourth term as Attorney General, instead filing to [[2026 United States House of Representatives election in South Dakota|run for Congress]] to represent [[South Dakota's at-large congressional district]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Dausch |first=Dominik |date=June 27, 2025 |title=Marty Jackley plans to run for US Rep. Dusty Johnson's job. Here's what we know |url=https://www.argusleader.com/story/news/politics/2025/06/27/marty-jackley-to-run-for-us-house-of-representatives-congress-south-dakota/84389067007/ |website=[[Argus Leader]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=staff |first=Dakota News Now |date=2026-04-01 |title=AG Marty Jackley qualifies for U.S. House of Representatives election ballot |url=https://www.dakotanewsnow.com/2026/04/01/ag-marty-jackley-qualifies-us-house-representatives-election-ballot/ |access-date=2026-04-01 |website=Dakota News Now |language=en}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Jackley was raised in [[Sturgis, South Dakota]], and graduated from [[Sturgis Brown High School]] in 1988.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://rapidcityjournal.com/news/local/communities/sturgis/jackley-says-states-best-days-lie-ahead/article_02ab8d93-a199-5f8b-9c78-ae3684918762.html |title=Jackley says state's best days lie ahead |first1=Deb |last1=Holland |work=Meade County Times-Tribune |date=October 10, 2017}}</ref> He graduated ''cum laude'' from the [[South Dakota School of Mines and Technology]] in 1992 with a [[Bachelor of Science]] in [[electrical engineering]]. He earned a [[Juris Doctor]] from the [[University of South Dakota School of Law]] in 1995.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.yankton.net/news/article_af62c8ae-8754-5c96-aaf7-edb599905853.html|title=U.S. Attorney Appointed S.D. Attorney General |date=August 20, 2009 |first=Chet |last=Brokaw |agency=Associated Press |website=Yankton Press & Dakotan}}</ref>

==Legal career==
From 1995 through 1997, Jackley served as a [[law clerk]] for then-Chief Judge [[Richard Battey]] of the [[United States District Court for the District of South Dakota]]. Jackley joined the [[Rapid City]] law firm Gunderson, Palmer, Nelson, and Ashmore.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.sdpb.org/blogs/kevinwoster/jackley-shows-up-for-branding-time-on-the-ranch-and-in-the-governors-race/ |title=It's branding time for Jackley - on the ranch and in the governor's race |publisher=SDPB |date= |accessdate=March 27, 2018}}</ref> As a partner at that firm, he focused his practice on [[construction law|construction]] & [[engineering law]] and real property disputes.  At that time, he also served as a Special Assistant Attorney General for South Dakota, prosecuting controlled substance felonies.

==United States Attorney (2006–2009)==
In 2006, Jackley was recommended by [[U.S. Senator]] [[John Thune]] to replace [[Steven K. Mullin]] as [[United States Attorney for the District of South Dakota]] and was nominated by President [[George W. Bush]].<ref name="rapidcityjournal1">{{cite web|url=http://rapidcityjournal.com/news/new-rapid-city-lawyer-nominated-as-u-s-attorney/article_fbc2f5fb-bde0-59c2-a355-f025c714a70d.html |title=NEW: Rapid City lawyer nominated as U.S. Attorney &#124; News |publisher=rapidcityjournal.com |date=May 17, 2006 |accessdate=March 27, 2018}}</ref> Jackley was [[unanimously]] confirmed by the U.S. Senate. In 2008, he was named the South Dakota Prosecutor of the Year by the South Dakota State's Attorneys Association. Jackley was succeeded as [[United States Attorney for the District of South Dakota|U.S. Attorney]] by [[Brendan Johnson]].

==Attorney General of South Dakota (2009–2019)==
Governor [[Mike Rounds]] appointed Jackley to succeed [[Larry Long (politician)|Larry Long]] as [[Attorney General of South Dakota]] in 2009 after Long was appointed as a local judge.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.drgnews.com/2013/11/27/jackley-discusses-possible-run-for-re-election|title=Jackley Discusses Possible Run for Re-Election|work=Drgnews|date=November 27, 2013|accessdate=January 10, 2014}}</ref> Jackley won reelection in 2010<ref>{{cite news|agency=Associated Press|url=http://www.kdlt.com/index.php?option=com_content&task=view&id=5896&Itemid=151|title=South Dakota News – Marty Jackley Voted S.D. Attorney General|publisher=Kdlt.com|date=November 2, 2010|accessdate=January 10, 2014}}</ref> and in [[2014 South Dakota Attorney General election|2014]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.argusleader.com/story/news/politics/2014/11/04/republicans-surging-statewide-races/18505051/|title=Statewide races: Jackley re-elected to AG|date=November 4, 2014|work=Argus Leader|accessdate=April 9, 2015}}</ref>

===Tenure===

====EB-5 Scandal====
[[EB-5]] was a national investor-visa program that granted green cards to undocumented immigrants and their families who have invested $500,000 in approved but not guaranteed investments.  South Dakota and Vermont were the only states that managed EB-5 funds through a state-controlled entity. 
On October 20, 2013, Richard Benda died from a gunshot wound.  Approximately a month and a half later, Jackley stated that the death was a suicide.  Initially it was questioned how a man could kill oneself with a shotgun.  An updated attorney general's report said, without any explanation, that a stick was used. Benda had served as Governor [[Mike Rounds]] director of economic development.  Nearly 3 years after Benda's death, Jackley charged Joop Bollen with five felony counts of unauthorized disposal of personal property to security interest.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.aberdeennews.com/news/local/bollen-charged-in-eb-5-case/article_d2a57947-a83b-5218-a403-5da68db718a6.html?redir=0 |title=Bollen charged in EB-5 case|website=aberdeennews.com|date=April 1, 2016|access-date=August 15, 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.keloland.com/news/eb-5-administrator-indicted-on-financial-misconduct-charges/|title=EB-5 administrator Indicted on Financial Misconduct Charges|website=keloland.com|date=May 10, 2016|access-date=August 15, 2021}}</ref> In February 2017, Bollen pleaded guilty to one count and was sentenced to a $2,000 fine and two years of probation.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://apnews.com/article/acf989193cb44189b7dd03fde6e0b122 |title= Deposition uncovers details about South Dakota visa scandal |publisher=apnews.com|date=October 20, 2018|access-date=August 15, 2021}}</ref>

====GEAR UP scandal====
On September 17, 2015, Scott Westerhuis shot and killed his four children, his wife, Nicole, and then set his house on fire, before killing himself.  Westerhuis was the business manager of Mid Central Educational Cooperative, which was contracted out by the state to distribute grant money. Hours before the Westerhuis home was found burning, Mid-Central Educational Cooperative, where Scott Westerhuis was the business manager, had lost a multi-million dollar state contract.  The decision by the state came after a series of financial problems turned up in audits of the business that administered a program that encourages Native American Students to go to college, called GEAR UP.<ref>{{cite web|url= https://www.keloland.com/investigates/gear-up/|title= GEAR UP |website=keloland.com|date= June 18, 2019 |access-date=August 15, 2021}}</ref>  Nearly, three years later in June 2018, Jackley lost the first of three possible GEAR UP cases as the jury acquitted Stephanie Hubers was found not guilty of grand theft, grand theft by deception and alternative receiving stolen property charges.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://apnews.com/article/0578f80873d54b9d985b50ef26eedc46|title=Jury clears South Dakota woman accused in embezzlement case|publisher=apnews.com|date=June 29, 2018|access-date=August 15, 2021}}</ref>  In September 2018, Jackley made a plea deal with Dan Guericke the former educational cooperative director, wherein Guericke pled guilty to one felony count of falsifying evidence.  Guericke had originally been charged with six felony counts alleging that he falsified evidence and conspired to offer forged or fraudulent evidence.  In October 2018, Jackley lost his second Gear Up jury trial when the jury acquitted Stacy Phelps, the former CEO of the American Institute for Innovation, on all charges.<ref>{{cite web|url= https://apnews.com/article/82b07f8a562f4a3fa1f4400683383998|title= South Dakota jury clears ex-nonprofit CEO in contracts case|publisher=aol.com|date=October 12, 2018|access-date=August 15, 2021}}</ref>

====Supported SB70, Adult Criminal Justice Reform law (2013)====
On January 18, 2013, Jackley testified before the Senate State Affairs Committee in support of SB 70.<ref>{{cite web|url= https://sdpb.sd.gov/SDPBPodcast/2013/sst08.mp3#t=189|title= House Judiciary Committee audio testimony regarding SB 70|website=sdpb.sd.gov|date=January 18, 2013|access-date=August 1, 2021}}</ref>  On February 6, 2013, Governor [[Dennis Daugaard]] signed SB 70 into law.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://sdlegislature.gov/Session/Bill/4057|title=Senate Bill 70|website=sdlegislature.gov |access-date=August 15, 2021}}</ref>

====Supported SB 73 Juvenile Criminal Justice Reform law (2015)====
On January 23, 2015, Jackley testified before the Senate State Affairs Committee in support of SB 73.<ref>{{cite web|url= https://sdpb.sd.gov/SDPBPodcast/2015/sst08.mp3#t=220|title=Senate Bill 73|website=sdlegislature.gov |access-date=August 15, 2021}}</ref>  On March 13, 2015, Governor Daugaard signed SB 73 into law.<ref>{{cite web|url= https://sdlegislature.gov/Session/Bill/6514|title=Senate Bill 73|website=sdlegislature.gov |access-date=August 15, 2021}}</ref>

====Annette Bosworth case====
On Wednesday, June 4, 2014, one day after losing the U.S. Senate primary, physician Annette Bosworth was arrested on charges of perjury and filing false documents, which charges were brought by Jackley.  Bosworth called the charges a “political intimidation scheme” against her by Jackley, who was appointed by then Governor and now U.S. Senator  [[Mike Rounds]] who just defeated Bosworth the day prior.<ref>{{cite web|url= https://www.aol.com/article/2014/06/04/south-dakota-candidate-charged-in-election-case/20906920/|title= South Dakota candidate charged in election case |publisher=aol.com|date=June 4, 2014|access-date=August 15, 2021}}</ref>  Many questioned why a plea deal could not be struck.  Bosworth stated “There’s no deal that will take away any of the felonies, so of course it’s going to trial”. “Paul Jacobs, a blogger who says he had experience with an overly aggressive prosecutor in Oklahoma over election issues several years ago. Jacobs says Jackley’s prosecution looks more like “persecution,” a line Bosworth repeats in her link to it.”  <ref>{{cite web|url= https://www.capjournal.com/news/bosworth-felony-trial-drawing-lots-of-interest/article_b59119f0-fd16-11e4-a5e5-9b80367b895a.html/|title= Bosworth felony trial drawing lots of interest |publisher=capjournal.com|date=May 17, 2015|access-date=August 15, 2021}}</ref>  Bosworth claimed that Jackley was prosecuting her for political and personal reasons.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.argusleader.com/story/davidmontgomery/2014/06/06/bosworth-news-conference/10066859//|title= Bosworth: Jackley has personal, political vendetta |publisher=argusleader.com |date=June 6, 2014|access-date=August 15, 2021}}</ref>  On May 27, 2015, Annette Bosworth was convicted via jury trial of six felonies for perjury and six felonies for filing false documents.<ref>{{cite web|url= https://www.foxnews.com/politics/former-gop-senate-candidate-convicted-of-violating-south-dakota-election-law|title= Former GOP Senate candidate convicted of violating South Dakota election law |website=foxnews.com|date=May 28, 2015|access-date=August 15, 2021}}</ref> On July 19, 2017, the South Dakota Supreme Court [[vacate]]d the six convictions for perjury, but affirmed the remaining convictions.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://ujs.sd.gov/uploads/sc/opinions/27510.pdf|title= State of South Dakota v. Annette Marie Bosworth|publisher=aberdeennews.com|date=July 19, 2017|access-date=August 15, 2021}}</ref> On November 3, 2017, Judge Jon Brown granted Bosworth a suspended imposition of sentence, which means she no longer has any felonies on her record.<ref>{{cite web|url= https://www.keloland.com/news/dr-bosworth-no-longer-has-felonies-on-her-record/|title= Dr. Bosworth No Longer Has Felonies On Her Record|publisher=keloland.com|date=November 3, 2017|access-date=August 15, 2021}}</ref>

====Flandreau marijuana case====
On August 3, 2016, Jackley filed 3 charges against Eric Hagen regarding conspiracy to possess, attempt to possess, and possession of more than 10 pounds of marijuana.<ref>{{cite web|url= https://www.blackhillsfox.com/content/news/Attorney-No-evidence-consultant-possessed-marijuana-390229772.html|title= Attorney: No evidence consultant possessed marijuana|website=blackhillsfox.com|date=August 15, 2016|access-date=August 15, 2021}}</ref>  On May 24, 2017, a jury acquitted Hagen of all charges.<ref>{{cite web|url= https://www.kob.com/us-news/latest-attorney-no-evidence-consultant-possessed-marijuana/4234409/|title= The Latest: Marijuana consultant: South Dakota had no case|website=keloland.com|date=May 24, 2017|access-date=August 1, 2021}}</ref>  The verdict was seen as a setback for Jackley in his bid for Governor.<ref>{{cite web|url= https://www.ksl.com/article/44369056/the-latest-south-dakota-ag-accepts-loss-in-drug-case|title= The latest: South Dakota AG accepts loss in drug case|date=May 24, 2017|access-date=August 15, 2021}}</ref>

====Gene Abdallah nomination====
On October 23, 2017, Jackley appointed [[South Dakota House of Representatives|state Representative]] [[Gene Abdallah]] to the state Board of Pardons and Paroles.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://atg.sd.gov/OurOffice/Media/pressreleasesdetail.aspx?id=1892|title=Gene Abdallah Appointed by Attorney General Jackley to Board of Pardons and Paroles|website=atg.sd.gov|date=October 23, 2017|access-date=August 15, 2021}}</ref>  On November 28, 2017, a former lobbyist, Tiffany Campbell, accused Abdallah of [[sexual harassment]] when he was in the legislature.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.blackhillsfox.com/content/news/former-lobbyist-460521143.html|title=Former lobbyist accused ex-lawmaker of sexual harassment |publisher=blackhillsfox.com|date=November 28, 2017|access-date=August 15, 2021}}</ref>  An appointment to the Board of Pardons and Parole must be confirmed by the state Senate <ref>{{cite web|url=https://sdlegislature.gov/Statutes/Codified_Laws/2049566|title=SDCL 24-13-1 Composition of board—Appointment of members|publisher=sdlegislature.gov|access-date=August 15, 2021}}</ref> As a result of the reports of sexual harassment, Abdallah withdrew from the Board of Pardons and Parole on January 16, 2018.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.argusleader.com/story/news/politics/2018/01/16/abdallah-withdraws-board-after-report-sexual-harassment/1033935001/|title= Abdallah Withdraws from the board after Report of Sexual Harassment |publisher=argusleader.com|date=January 16, 2018|access-date=August 15, 2021}}</ref>

====Laura Zylstra lawsuit====
In 2011, Division of Criminal Investigation (DCI) [an agency controlled by Jackley] agent, Laura Zylstra, filed a sexual harassment claim against a former Brown County deputy who made inappropriate comments towards her. Zylstra was then demoted and transferred from Aberdeen to Pierre. She then resigned in 2012. In September 2015, Zylstra sued DCI Director Bryan Gortmaker claiming she had been retaliated against with response to sexual harassment.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.aberdeennews.com/news/local/former-aberdeen-dci-agent-files-lawsuit/article_e8c46eb2-b460-5bd7-b5be-61a83aaaa798.html?redir=0 |title=DCI Agent files lawsuit: Litigation deals with response to sexual harassment |website=aberdeennews.com |date=September 25, 2015 |access-date=August 15, 2021 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210815132357/https://www.aberdeennews.com/news/local/former-aberdeen-dci-agent-files-lawsuit/article_e8c46eb2-b460-5bd7-b5be-61a83aaaa798.html?redir=0 |archive-date=August 15, 2021 }}</ref> In December 2017, the jury awarded Zylstra $1.2 million in damages finding that she had suffered retaliation and discrimination.<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.insurancejournal.com/news/midwest/2017/12/19/474808.htm |title=Former S.D. Law Enforcement Agent Awarded $1.2M in Discrimination Case |website=insurancejournal.com |date=December 19, 2017 |access-date=August 15, 2021  }}</ref> Zylstra thanked the jury for “giving me justice.”  She had alleged violations of the Civil Rights Act and the South Dakota Human Relations Act.<ref>{{cite web|url= https://www.keloland.com/news/judge-orders-dci-head-to-court-over-unpaid-1-5m-settlement/|title= Judge orders DCI Head to court over paid $1.5M settlement|website=keloland.com|date=May 22, 2018|access-date=August 15, 2021}}</ref> In May 2018, Federal District Court Judge [[Charles B. Kornmann]] ordered DCI Director, Bryan Gortmaker, to appear in court as the state failed to pay the $1.5M settlement.<ref>{{cite web|url= https://www.keloland.com/news/judge-orders-dci-head-to-court-over-unpaid-1-5m-settlement/|title= Judge orders DCI Head to court over paid $1.5M settlement|website=keloland.com|date=May 22, 2018|access-date=August 15, 2021}}</ref> Jackley claimed that the settlement was not being delayed and that Zylstra's lawyers and his  gubernatorial opponent [[Kristi Noem]] were playing politics.<ref>{{cite web|url= https://www.argusleader.com/story/news/2018/05/23/ex-dci-agent-marty-jackley-spar-over-facts-1-5-m-payout/637995002/|title= Ex-DCI Agent, Marty Jackley spar over "facts" in $1.5M payout|website=argusleader.com|date=May 23, 2018|access-date=August 15, 2021}}</ref>  Zylstra disputed in detail that there was a delay in the payments and personally appeared in campaign ads stating “I don’t think Marty Jackley should be Governor, I don’t think he should be the Attorney General”.<ref>{{cite web|url= https://www.dakotanewsnow.com/content/news/Former-DCI-agent-receives-15-million-settlement-payment-after-months-of-delay-483666591.html|title= Former DCI Agent receives $1.5 million settlement payment after months of delay|website=dakotanewsnow.com|date=May 24, 2018|access-date=August 15, 2021}}</ref>

==2018 gubernatorial election==
{{Main|2018 South Dakota gubernatorial election}}

===Candidates===
In November 2016, Jackley declared his intention to seek the Republican nomination for [[Governor of South Dakota]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.argusleader.com/story/news/politics/2016/11/15/marty-jackley-moves-700k-toward-governor-run/93917232/|title=Marty Jackley moves $700K toward governor run|publisher=argusleader.com|date=November 15, 2016|access-date=July 15, 2021}}</ref>  Congresswoman [[Kristi Noem]] also declared that she would seek the Republican nomination for governor.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.politico.com/story/2016/11/kristi-noem-south-dakota-231386|title=Rep. Kristi Noem to run for South Dakota governor |work=Politico.com|date=November 14, 2016|access-date=July 6, 2021}}</ref> Terry LaFleur <ref>{{cite web|url=https://ballotpedia.org/Terry_Lee_Lafleur|title=Terry Lee LaFleur|work=Ballotpedia.org|access-date=July 15, 2021 }}</ref> and Lora Hubel also declared their intention to seek the Republican nomination for governor, however, LaFleur & Hubel were unable to obtain the required number of signatures to make the primary ballot.<ref>{{cite web|url= https://ballotpedia.org/Lora_Hubbel |title=Lora Hubbell|work=Ballotpedia.org|access-date=July 15, 2021}}</ref>

===Debates===
Jackley and Noem participated in three debates.

====First debate====
In the first debate both candidates tried to define the other.  Jackley stated: “It’s Washington experience versus South Dakota experience.” “Marty’s background has been being a government lawyer,” Noem said.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.capjournal.com/news/jackley-and-noem-battle-in-tv-debate/article_3505d2d2-62d3-11e8-bf67-c340e734ec61.html |title= Jackley and Noem battle in TV debate| publisher=capjournal.com|date=May 28, 2018 |access-date=July 6, 2021}}</ref>

====Second debate====
In the second debate, Noem discussed Marty's scandals.  “In EB5, the state oversight program, nobody went to jail. On Gear-Up, still, nobody’s been punished. When we talk about what’s been going on in Brookings with the Global Aquaponics scam—a con artist, Tobias Ritesman, held a fundraiser for Marty Jackley. Marty attended his phony groundbreaking for his phony project,” Noem says. “People lost hundreds of thousands of dollars. Still, nobody’s been investigated and nobody’s been prosecuted. That needs to change in our state.”

Jackley was thrown on the defensive during the second debate.  “Congresswoman, he didn’t hold a fundraiser for me. I was at an event that he was at, and I did go to a ground breaking because that’s what important in South Dakota,” Jackley says. “When we have businesses expanding I think it’s important that we attend those. You talk about Gear-Up, there hasn’t been a sentencing because these defendants are presumed innocent. But I as attorney general, unlike Washington, have done something about it. I actually formed a grand jury. Indictments have been issued. They’re schedule to begin jury trials in July—or, excuse me—June, June 26th and I plan on trying those personally, because that’s what a leader does.”  <ref>{{cite web|url=https://listen.sdpb.org/post/gop-governor-candidates-spar-over-transparency-during-sdpb-tv-debate|title= GOP Governor Candidates Spar Over Transparency During SDPB TV Debate| publisher=sdpb.org|date=May 30, 2018 |access-date=July 6, 2021}}</ref>

====Final debate====
In the final debate, Jackley and Noem took questions about workforce development, anti-discrimination laws, drugs, uniting democrats and republicans in the state to make critical decisions and much more. A subject of disagreement was the state's 134 boards and commissions. Noem said she wanted to streamline different processes for licensure, eliminating "red tape" but Jackley disagreed.  "Every time that a proposal comes forward to create a new 'blue ribbon' task force, a board or a commission, what typically comes with that is another layer of bureaucracy," Noem said.  Jackley defended the government bureaucracy.  "We need a governor that understands that various different boards, isn't out there criticizing different boards and saying that type of service isn't important," Jackley said.  Jackley spoke about putting together a task force to work on government transparency and open records laws.  "I'm committed when I become governor to put forth a taskforce ...because we need to take a look at the open records law," he said.  They both ended the debate with a jab at the other.  "It really comes to down to Washington experience versus South Dakota experience," Jackley said. "The congresswoman has been spending considerable time and effort talking about Marty Jackley, but I'm talking about you, South Dakota."  "Days ago he stood up and talked about protecting victims while behind the scenes he was actively working to silence one to further his political career," Noem said. "You deserve a governor who will be honest with you, who will tell you the truth and who is willing to be accountable."  <ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.dakotanewsnow.com/content/news/Jackley-Noem-face-off-in-final-contentious-debate-before-primary-election-484245331.html|title= Jackley, Noem face-off in final contentious debate before primary election| publisher=dakotanewsnow.com|date=May 31, 2018 |access-date=July 6, 2021}}</ref>

====Primary results====
Jackley lost in the [[South Dakota gubernatorial election, 2018|June primary]] to U.S. Representative [[Kristi Noem]].  Jackley only won 7 of South Dakota's 66 counties.  Jackley received 45,069 (44%) votes and Noem received 57,437 (56%) votes.<ref name="SDSOS06062018">[http://electionresults.sd.gov/resultsSW.aspx?type=SWR&map=CTY State of South Dakota Secretary of State Official Election Results], June 5, 2018.</ref>

==Private sector (2019–2022)==
After the election, Jackley rejoined the firm of Gunderson, Palmer, Nelson and Ashmore and opened up a law office in [[Pierre, South Dakota]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://rapidcityjournal.com/news/local/jackley-will-open-pierre-office-for-rapid-city-law-firm/article_a637181c-3d80-556e-b411-8afefa607bc8.html|title=Jackley will open Pierre office for Rapid City law firm|publisher=rapidcityjournal.com|date=November 20, 2018|accessdate=May 26, 2019}}</ref> On August 27, 2019, Jackley was sworn in as the Jones County States Attorney after he was appointed to fill the vacancy left when  Anita Fuoss resigned.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://gpna.com/news/marty-jackley-becomes-jones-county-states-attorney| title=Marty Jackley becomes Jones County States Attorney| publisher=gpna.com|date=August 28, 2019 |accessdate=August 29, 2019}}</ref> He did not run for a full term and was succeeded by Kirby Krogman in January 2021.<ref>{{cite news |last=Tisone |first=Michael |date=November 4, 2020 |title=2020 South Dakota Election Results |url=https://kwyr.com/2020-south-dakota-election-results/?doing_wp_cron=1626868755.3136610984802246093750 |work=KWYR Radio |location=Winner, SD}}</ref>

===Measure 24===
In 2017, an initiated measure was started to ban financial contributions from out of state residents, political committees and entities to ballot question committees.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://ballotpedia.org/South_Dakota_Initiated_Measure_24,_Ban_Out-of-State_Contributions_to_Ballot_Question_Committees_Initiative_(2018)|title= South Dakota Initiated Measure 24, Ban Out-of-State Contributions to Ballot Question Committees Initiative (2018)|publisher=Ballotpedia.org|accessdate=July 12, 2021}}</ref>  On June 14, 2017, the Legislative Research Counsel, proposed edits to the Initiated Measure.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://sdsos.gov/elections-voting/assets/Ballot%20Question%20Documents/2018/2018_IM_LRCComments_ProhibitContributionsToBQs.pdf |title= An Act to prohibit contributions to ballot question committees by out-of-state residents, political committees, and entities and to establish civil penalties therefor.|publisher=sdsos.gov|date=June 14, 2017|accessdate=July 12, 2021}}</ref> On July 31, 2017, Jackley, while serving as Attorney General, submitted his Attorney General's explanation regarding IM 24 to the Secretary of State pursuant to SDCL 12-13-25.1.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://sdsos.gov/electionsvoting/assets/Ballot%20Question%20Documents/2018/2018_IM_ProhibContBQ_AGStatement.pdf |title= Attorney General's Statement for initiated measure (prohibiting contributions to ballot question committees by non-residents, out-of-state political committees, and entities that are not filed with the Secretary of State) |publisher=sdsos.gov|date=July 31, 2017|accessdate=July 12, 2021}}</ref> IM 24 passed with 174,960 (55.52%) votes for the initiated measure and 140,172 (44.48%) votes against it.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://sdsos.gov/elections-voting/assets/2018GeneralElectionCanvassPDF.pdf|title=2018 General Election Official Results State Canvas|publisher=sdsos.gov|date=November 13, 2018|accessdate=July 12, 2021|archive-date=April 21, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210421035854/https://sdsos.gov/elections-voting/assets/2018GeneralElectionCanvassPDF.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>  On March 4, 2019, South Dakota Voice, a grassroots ballot question committee, headed by Cory Heidelberger, filed a lawsuit to stop IM 24.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.keloland.com/news/lawsuit-filed-against-south-dakota-officials-to-stop-im-24/|title= Lawsuit Filed Against South Dakota Officials To Stop IM 24 |publisher=keloland.com|date=March 4, 2019|accessdate=July 12, 2021}}</ref> On April 17, 2019, a complaint was filed against the state to invalidate IM 24 by Jackley approximately six weeks after initial lawsuit by Heidelberger and despite having written the Attorney General explanation for the state.<ref>{{cite web|url=
https://www.ifs.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/SD-Compaint-4.17.pdf
|title= Complaint |publisher=ifs.org|date=April 17, 2019|accessdate=July 12, 2021}}</ref> On May 9, 2019, Federal Judge Charles Kornmann struck down IM 24.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://listen.sdpb.org/post/ban-out-state-money-ballot-questions-overturned
|title= Ban On Out-Of-State Money To Ballot Questions Overturned
|publisher=sdpb.org|date=May 9, 2019|accessdate=August 16, 2021}}</ref> South Dakota Voice was awarded attorney fees from the state in the amount of $32,100; expenses in the amount of $1,083.90 and costs in the amount of $505.40.  Jackley was awarded attorney fees for his clients nearly three times of South Dakota Voice in the amount of $79,640.00, despite starting six weeks after the South Dakota Voice complaint.<ref>SD Voice and Cory Heidelberger v. Noem et al, Case No. 1:19-cv-01003-CBK; South Dakota Newspaper Association et al v. Barnett et al, 3:19-CV-03010, Document 51, filed January 9, 2020|access-date= July 13, 2021</ref>

===Representation of T. Denny Sanford===

In 2020, it was reported that [[T. Denny Sanford]], the richest man in South Dakota, was being investigated for possession of child pornography.  Sanford was represented by Jackley.<ref>{{cite web|title= T. Denny Sanford subject of child pornography investigation|url=https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/crime/t-denny-sanford-subject-of-child-pornography-investigation/ar-BB18vcsW|website=msn.com|date=August 29, 2020|access-date=July 13, 2021}}</ref>  Investigators obtained a search warrant before referring the case to the [[United States Department of Justice]].<ref>{{cite web|last1=Faturechi|first1=Robert|first2=Isaac|last2=Arnsdorf|title=Billionaire T. Denny Sanford Was Under Investigation for Child Pornography|url=https://www.propublica.org/article/billionaire-t-denny-sanford-was-under-investigation-for-child-pornography?token=l24Nh-wDyBgy53bhcy5jGvQh1IDRcxzE|website=ProPublica|date=August 28, 2020|access-date=July 14, 2021|archive-date=August 11, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220811055526/https://www.propublica.org/article/billionaire-t-denny-sanford-was-under-investigation-for-child-pornography?token=l24Nh-wDyBgy53bhcy5jGvQh1IDRcxzE|url-status=dead}}</ref> The investigation has led several institutions towards reconsideration of his philanthropy.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2020-09-04|title=National University holds off on name change after reports of T. Denny Sanford investigation|url=https://www.lajollalight.com/news/story/2020-09-04/reports-child-porn-investigation-denny-sanford-san-diego|access-date=2021-01-03|website=La Jolla Light}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last=Fugleberg |first=Jeremy |date=August 31, 2020 |title=Sanford Health distances itself from child porn investigation into top patron T. Denny Sanford: 'This matter does not involve our health system'|url=https://www.duluthnewstribune.com/newsmd/health-news/6640049-Sanford-Health-distances-itself-from-child-porn-investigation-into-top-patron-T.-Denny-Sanford-This-matter-does-not-involve-our-health-system|access-date=2021-01-03|website=Duluth News Tribune}}</ref>

On October 27, 2021, the South Dakota Supreme Court unanimously ruled against the "Implicated Individual" that search warrants that were sought will be unsealed, pending any motion(s) for rehearing.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://ujs.sd.gov/uploads/sc/opinions/294736a211b3.pdf|title=In the matter of the Appeal of an Implicated Individual, 2021 S.D. 61|date=October 27, 2021|accessdate=November 24, 2021}}</ref>  On November 17, 2021, the South Dakota Supreme Court unsealed records confirming that T. Denny Sanford was the implicated individual and that five search warrants were issued during the investigation.  The documents included the contents of the warrants, the return of the warrant and the inventory dating back to 2019.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://news.yahoo.com/warrants-sought-t-denny-sanfords-230709199.html|title=Warrants sought T. Denny Sanford's email, data records in S.D. child pornography investigation|date=November 17, 2021|accessdate=November 24, 2021}}</ref>

==Attorney General of South Dakota (2023–present)==
===2022 attorney general election===
{{See also|2022 South Dakota Attorney General election}}
On March 1, 2021, Jackley announced that he would run for attorney general in the 2022 election.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.argusleader.com/story/news/2021/03/01/marty-jackley-jason-ravnsborg-2022-south-dakota-attorney-general/6870648002/|title=Marty Jackley announces run for S.D. attorney general as Jason Ravnsborg faces impeachment|first=Joe|last=Sneve|website=Argus Leader}}</ref> He won the general election unopposed.

==Personal life==
Jackley lives in [[Pierre, South Dakota]], with his two children, Michael and Isabella.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.argusleader.com/story/news/politics/2014/04/07/marty-jackley-will-seek-re-election-attorney-general/7414075/|title=Marty Jackley will seek re-election as attorney general|website=argusleader.com|accessdate=July 28, 2017}}</ref>
